passages.happening:
Six days after Peter's confession, Jesus takes Peter, James and John up a high mountain, away from everyone. There he is changed before them. “His face shone like the sun, and His clothes became as white as the light” (verse 2). Moses and Elijah appear and talk with him.

Peter offers to put up three shelters, one for each of them. While he is still speaking, a bright cloud covers them, and a voice from the cloud says, “This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to Him!” (verse 5). The disciples fall face down in terror. Jesus comes over and touches them. “Get up,” he says. “Do not be afraid.” When they look up, they see no one except Jesus.
passages.hearers:
Mark tells this same scene, and the note on Mark 9 explains the shelters, the Feast of Tabernacles behind them, and the old question of which mountain it was. No one can be sure. Here it is worth noticing what Matthew does differently.

Only Matthew says Jesus' face “shone like the sun”. Only he calls the cloud bright. Only he gives the voice the words “in whom I am well pleased”, so that they match the voice at Jesus' baptism exactly: “This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased!” (3:17). The same Father says the same thing at the start of Jesus' work and now, on the road to the cross.

Matthew also names Moses before Elijah (Mark has “Elijah and Moses”). And in Matthew, Peter calls Jesus ‘Lord’, where in Mark he says ‘Rabbi’, a teacher.

The last part is Matthew's alone. The three fall on their faces in terror, and Jesus comes and touches them and tells them to get up and not be afraid. The glory frightens them. The same Jesus who shone like the sun puts his hand on their shoulders.

Years later Peter remembered this night. His second letter says, “we ourselves heard this voice from heaven when we were with Him on the holy mountain” (2 Peter 1:18).
passages.ot:
Moses on Mount Sinai stands behind almost every detail. A cloud covered the mountain for six days, and God spoke from it (Exodus 24:16). When Moses came down, “his face had become radiant from speaking with the LORD” (Exodus 34:29). The difference matters. Moses' face shone because he had been with God. Jesus' face shines from within.

The voice gathers three Old Testament promises into one sentence. ‘My Son’ is what God says to his king in Psalm 2:7: “You are My Son.” ‘In whom I am well pleased’ recalls God's servant: “Here is My Servant, whom I uphold, My Chosen One, in whom My soul delights” (Isaiah 42:1). And ‘Listen to Him’ is Moses' own word about the prophet God would send: “You must listen to him” (Deuteronomy 18:15).

The fall, the touch and the words ‘Do not be afraid’ echo the prophet Daniel. When a heavenly messenger spoke to him, Daniel fell with his face to the ground, and “a hand touched me”, and he was told, “Do not be afraid, Daniel” (Daniel 10:9-12).
passages.asks: When the cloud lifted, “they saw no one except Jesus” (verse 8). Moses and Elijah, the Law and the Prophets, had pointed to him and then stepped back. Ask what else is crowding your view of Jesus, and what it would mean this week to do the one thing the voice commanded: listen to him.

passages.t: Coming down: Elijah has already come
passages.happening: On the way down, Jesus tells them, “Do not tell anyone about this vision until the Son of Man has been raised from the dead” (verse 9). The disciples ask why the scribes say Elijah must come first. Jesus answers that Elijah does come and will restore all things. But Elijah has already come, and they did not recognize him and did to him whatever they wished. The Son of Man will suffer at their hands in the same way. Then the disciples understand that he is speaking about John the Baptist.
passages.hearers:
The question about Elijah, and the waiting for him, is explained in the note on Mark 9. Malachi had promised that Elijah would come before the great day of the Lord, and people were watching for him.

Matthew adds one sentence Mark does not have: the disciples understood that he meant John the Baptist (verse 13). Jesus had already said so to the crowds: “he is the Elijah who was to come” (11:14). Now the three disciples see it too.

Matthew calls what they saw a ‘vision’. The Greek word, horama, means something seen, a sight God shows. Acts uses it of the burning bush that Moses saw (Acts 7:31). It does not mean a dream or something unreal. It means God let them see.

Why keep it secret until he was raised? Before the cross, talk of a shining Messiah would only feed the wrong hopes. People wanted a king who would win. The glory could be understood only after the suffering.
passages.ot:
The promise comes from the last lines of the Prophets: “Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and awesome Day of the LORD” (Malachi 4:5). Malachi said Elijah would “turn the hearts of the fathers to their children” (Malachi 4:6). John did that kind of work, calling people back to God.

The pattern of rejection is old too. Elijah was hunted by Queen Jezebel (1 Kings 19:2). John was killed in Herod's prison (14:1-12). Jesus says the same road lies ahead for him.
passages.asks: The disciples came down from a mountaintop with a question about prophecy, and Jesus answered with suffering. Ask whether you want the glory of following Jesus more than the road he walked to reach it.

passages.t: A boy with seizures, and faith the size of a mustard seed
passages.happening:
At the foot of the mountain a man comes and kneels before Jesus. “Lord, have mercy on my son,” he says. “He has seizures and is suffering terribly. He often falls into the fire or into the water” (verse 15). He brought the boy to the disciples, but they could not heal him.

Jesus says, “O unbelieving and perverse generation!” and asks how long he must put up with them. “Bring the boy here to Me.” Jesus rebukes the demon. It comes out of the boy, and he is healed from that moment.

Later the disciples ask in private why they could not drive it out. “Because you have so little faith,” Jesus answers. If you have faith the size of a mustard seed, you can say to this mountain, ‘Move from here to there,’ and it will move. “Nothing will be impossible for you” (verse 20).

Your Bible may go straight from verse 20 to verse 22. That is explained below.
passages.hearers:
Mark tells this story at length, with the father's great cry, “I do believe; help my unbelief!” (Mark 9:24). Matthew tells it in a few verses. He leaves out the father's struggle and puts the weight on the disciples' failure and on what Jesus says about faith.

Matthew's word for the boy's illness is unusual. The Greek word, selēniazomai, comes from the word for the moon. It means ‘moonstruck’, because people thought seizures came and went with the moon. Older English Bibles turned it into ‘lunatic’. Today we would call what the father describes seizures, and Bibles such as the BSB say so. Matthew uses this word only twice. The other time is in his list of the people Jesus healed, where “the demon-possessed” and “those having seizures” are named as different needs (4:24). Greek doctors had long argued that seizures have natural causes. The note on Mark 9 tells more.

Jesus had already used the mustard seed for the kingdom's small beginning, calling it “the smallest of all seeds” (13:32). It stood for the smallest thing there is. Moving a mountain was a way of saying ‘doing what cannot be done’. Paul uses the same picture: “absolute faith so as to move mountains” (1 Corinthians 13:2).
passages.ot: Jesus' cry, “O unbelieving and perverse generation”, takes up Moses' words about Israel in his last song: “a perverse and crooked generation” (Deuteronomy 32:5). It also recalls the day Moses came down from Sinai and found the people at the foot of the mountain worshipping a golden calf (Exodus 32:19). The pattern repeats: glory above, failure below.
passages.hard:
Does this story mean that seizures, or illness of the mind, are caused by demons? Christians hold that evil is real, and the Gospels tell of real possession. But most Christians today hold that seizures and mental illness are illnesses, to be treated with medicine and care, and that it is wrong and harmful to tell a sick person they have a demon. The Gospels themselves know the difference. Matthew himself lists those having seizures apart from the demon-possessed (4:24).

The father says his son often falls into the fire or into the water. If you, or someone you love, are at risk of harm, reach for real help now: a doctor, a pastor you trust, or a crisis line in your country. Jesus did not leave this boy alone, and you are not meant to face such danger alone.

Does verse 20 mean that anyone with enough faith will be healed, and that someone who stays ill did not believe enough? No. The Bible does not teach that sickness comes from too little faith, or that a person who stays ill did not believe enough. Notice whose faith Jesus speaks of here. Not the boy's, and not the father's. It is the disciples' faith that falls short, and Jesus heals the boy anyway. And the point of the mustard seed is that it is tiny. Jesus is not setting a level of faith that a person must reach to get results. Faith is trust in a person, not a payment that buys a cure. Its power is in the God it trusts, not in how strongly it is felt. This verse is not a formula, and it should never be used to blame anyone for an illness that has not gone away.

Verse 21. Older Bibles, such as the King James Version, have a verse here: ‘this kind goes out only by prayer and fasting’. The oldest copies of Matthew, among them the first hand of Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, do not have it. Most scholars think a copyist added it from Mark 9:29, and the words ‘and fasting’ are missing from the oldest copies of Mark too. So the BSB, like most modern Bibles, leaves the number 21 empty and gives the words in a footnote. Some Christians who hold to the later copies think the verse belongs. Nothing in Christian teaching turns on it; prayer and fasting are taught in other places (6:5-18).
passages.asks: Jesus did not tell the disciples to try harder or to feel more certain. He told them that even a speck of real trust in God is enough, because God does the moving. Ask where your faith feels too small to matter. Then bring it to him anyway, small as it is.

passages.t: The second warning: killed and raised
passages.happening: When they gather in Galilee, Jesus tells them, “The Son of Man is about to be delivered into the hands of men. They will kill Him, and on the third day He will be raised to life” (verses 22-23). And the disciples are deeply grieved.
passages.hearers:
This is the second of Jesus' three warnings about his death. The first was in 16:21, and the third will come in 20:17-19. This one is the shortest.

Notice how the disciples respond. In Mark, “they did not understand this statement, and they were afraid to ask Him about it” (Mark 9:32). In Matthew they are ‘deeply grieved’. They have understood enough to be sad. They have heard ‘they will kill him’. They have not yet taken in ‘he will be raised’.

‘Delivered’ means handed over. The same word will be used of Judas handing Jesus over (26:15-16) and of Pilate handing him over to be crucified (27:26). Behind them all, Christians have heard God's own purpose. Paul says Jesus “was delivered over to death for our trespasses” (Romans 4:25), using the same word.
passages.ot: Isaiah's suffering servant was handed over to death: “He was pierced for our transgressions, He was crushed for our iniquities” (Isaiah 53:5). And the hope of being raised ‘on the third day’ has an echo in the prophet Hosea: “on the third day He will raise us up, that we may live in His presence” (Hosea 6:2).
passages.asks: The disciples heard the death and missed the rising. Grief was the right first response, and Jesus does not scold them for it. Ask whether, in your own sorrow, you have heard the whole sentence, the death and the promise after it.

passages.t: The temple tax and the coin in the fish
passages.happening:
Back in Capernaum, the men who collect the two-drachma tax come to Peter. “Does your Teacher pay the two drachmas?” “Yes,” Peter says.

When Peter comes into the house, Jesus speaks first. “What do you think, Simon?” From whom do the kings of the earth take customs and taxes: from their own sons, or from others? “From others,” Peter answers. “Then the sons are exempt,” Jesus says.

“But so that we may not offend them,” he goes on, go to the sea, cast a hook, and take the first fish. In its mouth you will find a four-drachma coin. “Take it and give it to them for My tax and yours” (verse 27).

This story is told only in Matthew.
passages.hearers:
The ‘two drachmas’ was the yearly tax for the temple in Jerusalem. A drachma was a Greek silver coin. Two drachmas made a half shekel, the sum the Law of Moses names. By Jesus' day Jewish men paid it every year to keep up the temple's daily worship. Jews who lived far away paid it too. The historian Josephus tells how Jews in Babylon kept the money in two strong cities, Nehardea and Nisibis, until it could be carried to Jerusalem. The Mishnah, written down around AD 200, remembers how it was gathered: money changers set up their tables in the towns in the month of Adar, and later in the temple itself (Shekalim 1:3).

The coin Peter finds is a stater, a four-drachma silver coin. One of them paid the tax for two men, Jesus and Peter. The coin used for temple payments was usually the silver shekel minted at Tyre.

Matthew's first readers would have heard this story with fresh ears. After the Romans destroyed the temple in AD 70, the emperor Vespasian ordered every Jew to pay the same two drachmas each year to the temple of Jupiter in Rome (Josephus, Jewish War 7.218). If Matthew wrote after AD 70, as most scholars think, his readers knew what it was to pay this sum.

Jesus' question about kings uses a picture everyone knew. Kings taxed the peoples they ruled, not their own families. The temple was God's house. Jesus is the Son of the king whose house it is. So he does not owe the tax. He pays it anyway.
passages.ot:
The half shekel comes from Exodus 30. When Israel was counted, each man was to give a half shekel to the LORD as “a ransom for his life” (Exodus 30:12). It was the same for everyone: “the rich shall not give more than a half shekel, nor shall the poor give less” (Exodus 30:15). The money paid for “the service of the Tent of Meeting” (Exodus 30:16). After the exile, the people promised “to contribute a third of a shekel yearly for the service of the house of our God” (Nehemiah 10:32).

Jesus has already said that “something greater than the temple is here” (12:6). Here the Son pays the tax for his Father's house.
passages.hard:
Did a fish really carry a coin? Skeptics point out that the story is found only in Matthew, and that Matthew never actually says Peter caught the fish. They also point to old tales of treasure found in fish. The Greek historian Herodotus tells how Polycrates, a ruler of Samos, threw his precious ring into the sea and found it days later inside a fish (Histories 3.41-42). So some readers think a folk tale has been joined to a true saying of Jesus. Others, from the early church onward, have read it as a real miracle. John Chrysostom, a preacher of the late 300s, said in his sermons on Matthew that Jesus first shows he is not bound to pay and then pays anyway, so that no one would stumble, and pays for Peter as well. Many readers also notice that the story is told for what Jesus says, not for the fish. As with other miracles, the answer turns in part on whether God acts in the world at all. These notes do not decide it.

One more thing should be said plainly. This passage is about the temple tax, a gift for the worship of God's house. It is not a teaching about modern taxes, about any government, or about what Christians owe the state. The New Testament speaks to that in other places (22:21; Romans 13:7), and Christians read those places in more than one way. Nor is the coin a promise that God will send money to anyone who needs it.
passages.asks: Jesus was free, and he still gave up his right so as not to put a stumbling block in anyone's way. Paul learned the same: “Though I am free of obligation to anyone, I make myself a slave to everyone” (1 Corinthians 9:19). Ask what right you are holding on to that you could lay down, for the sake of someone else's faith.
